newsitem.title: USA: Tight election seen for new Republican chairman.
newsitem.headline: Tight election seen for new Republican chairman.

text.p: After a bruising, occasionally dirty campaign, the Republican Party will choose its new chairman on Friday in an election expected to require several ballots.
With the candidates spending hundreds of thousands of dollars on campaign videos, mailings and travel, the election has turned into a fight for the soul of the Republican Party.

Eight candidates are vying to succeed Haley Barbour, the folksy Mississippian who won much of the credit when the Republicans gained control of both houses of Congress in 1994 and retained that advantage in last November's election.

The new party leader will be picked by 165 members of the Republican National Committee -- three from each state and the rest from the District of Columbia and various U.S. territories. Eighty three votes are required for election.

The job of chairman has become increasingly important as party organisations wield ever-greater amounts of campaign funds. The chairman's duties also include frequent television appearances as well as fundraising and organisation.
The new chairman will prepare Republicans for the 1998 mid-term elections, when many expect them to strengthen their control of Congress, and for the presidential election in the year 2000.
President Bill Clinton this week chose Colorado Gov. Roy Romer as Democratic Party chairman and Massachusetts businessman Steve Grossman to run day-to-day party operations.
Best known of the Republican candidates is former New Hampshire Gov. Steve Merrill. The other candidates are either past or present party functionaries.
Merrill has run into strong opposition from conservatives, who say he is too closely associated with Bob Dole's failed 1996 presidential bid.

Last week, all 165 committee members received unsigned mailings suggesting that infidelity to his third wife forced Merrill not to seek re-election as New Hampshire governor. The mailings included photocopies of his two divorce decrees.
"I've never seen anything like this. It has usually been very gentlemanly but this has really turned nasty," said Delaware Republican chairman Basil Battaglia.
Carrying the banner of the right-wing and the powerful Christian Coalition is Tom Pauken, Texas Republican chairman who is a strong opponent of abortion and an advocate of traditional values.
David Norcross, the Republican national committee's counsel, is seen as a more moderate alternative who is a qualified supporter of abortion rights.

If none of these can muster enough support, committee members may turn to Colorado chairman Jim Nicholson or Ohio chairman Bob Bennett. The other candidates -- California chairman John Herrington, Florida's Jeanie Austin and Chuck Yob of Michigan -- start the race as long-shot candidates.

A straw poll last week by the Hotline political newsletter showed Merrill and Norcross the early leaders. But neither had anywhere enough votes to win on a first ballot and most analysts expect the election to go at least three and possibly more rounds before a winner emerges.
